newsitem.title: UK: S&P sets Banco Provincial CP ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P sets Banco Provincial CP ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Wednesday it had assigned its BB minus local currency counterparty credit rating and B foreign currency counterparty credit rating to Banco Provincial S.A., Caracas.
"The ratings reflect Banco Provincial's dominant position in the Venezuelan banking market, good financial indicators, and capable management," S&P said in a statement.
S&P said the outlook on Banco Provincial's foreign currency debt was stable, matching the outlook on the Republic of Venezuela's foreign currency debt.
"All things being equal, a change in the rating or outlook of the Republic would also prompt a similar change in the rating or outlook of Banco Provincial," S&P said.
It said the outlook on Banco Provincial's local currency debt was also stable.

"S&P expects bank industry risk to decline gradually from its high level in Venezuela as regulators re-establish credibility in their supervision. However, this new, more propitious environment also will become more competitive," S&P said. "On balance, S&P sees Banco Provincial's credit standing remaining stable thanks to its current position of strength in the Venezuelan market."

S&P said the ratings incorporated the difficult operating environment of Venezuela, whose assistance to the banking sector had cost the government to date upwards of 22 percent of 1994 GDP since the crisis began in January of that year, as well as the prospect for increased competition resulting from the likely sale of state-owned Banco de Venezuela and Banco Consolidado into foreign hands.

"The local currency rating of Banco Provincial is not constrained by the rating of the Republic of Venezuela, whose local currency debt is not publicly rated by Standard & Poor's," the rating agency said.

"The Republic is currently in default on roughly 60 billion Bolivars (US$125 million) of Bonos de la Deuda Publica National. Standard & Poor's views the Republic's default --which is expected to be cured shortly-- as a technical issue related to the central government's own debt management and not symptomatic of economic collapse," S&P said.
